notes: Brandt's real partner, the FDP, sits in slot 2 instead of MD's slot 16 because 16 has no starting popularity. The template coalition slot 18 holds the Jusos, the SPD youth wing that turned left in December 1969, as the nearest partner. The CSU is split off from the CDU into slot 14 as Bavaria's regional party. MD's slot-22 DVU was only founded in 1971; the Bundeswehr takes slot 22. Slot 7 is the banned KPD apparatus and slot 13 the Bundesbank.

0.name: Bundesnachrichtendienst
0.text:
The Federal Intelligence Service grew out of the Gehlen Organization, which the former Wehrmacht general Reinhard Gehlen built for the Americans after 1946 and which passed under federal control in 1956. Since Gehlen's retirement in 1968 it has been led by General Gerhard Wessel from its walled compound at Pullach near Munich, still scarred by the Felfe affair of 1961, when a Soviet mole was unmasked in its ranks.

The service sees the Federal Republic as the front line against the Soviet bloc and works hand in glove with the CIA, running agents in the GDR and a secret stay-behind network for the event of invasion. Many officers distrust Brandt's opening to the East. Its leverage lies in files, foreign patrons and the networks of an anti-communist emergency state.

1.name: Christlich Demokratische Union Deutschlands
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Union has led every federal government since 1949 but was pushed into opposition in October 1969, although together with its Bavarian sister party it remains the largest group in the Bundestag with 46.1 percent. Its chairman, the former Chancellor Kurt Georg Kiesinger, is a weakened figure, while the parliamentary leader Rainer Barzel and younger reformers such as Helmut Kohl in Mainz vie for the future.

The party embodies Adenauer's legacy of Western integration, NATO, European unity and Erhard's social market economy, and it attacks Brandt's Ostpolitik as a surrender of German rights in the East. Its base lies among Catholics, farmers, the middle classes, expellees and business, and its leverage rests on its narrow majority in the Bundesrat and its strength in the states.

2.name: Freie Demokratische Partei
2.text:
The Free Democratic Party, the heir of German liberalism, won only 5.8 percent in 1969 but holds the balance of power. Its chairman Walter Scheel took it into a coalition with the Social Democrats and became Foreign Minister and Vice-Chancellor, with Hans-Dietrich Genscher at the Interior Ministry, while its national-liberal right around the former leader Erich Mende fumes at the change of course.

The party stands for civil liberties, secular schools, legal reform, free enterprise and a pragmatic Ostpolitik of reconciliation with Poland and the East within the Western alliance. Its voters are professionals, the self-employed and the educated Protestant middle class. Its leverage lies in its role as kingmaker: without its thirty seats neither big party can govern.

3.name: Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party of Germany, founded in 1863, heads a German government for the first time since 1930. Willy Brandt, its chairman since 1964 and former Mayor of West Berlin, was elected Chancellor on 21 October 1969 with a slender majority, flanked by the parliamentary leader Herbert Wehner, Defence Minister Helmut Schmidt and Economics Minister Karl Schiller.

Under the motto 'Dare more democracy' it promises reforms in education, law and co-determination and a new Ostpolitik that accepts the realities of post-war Europe, seeks treaties with Moscow, Warsaw and East Berlin and has already signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty, all firmly anchored in NATO. A people's party since Bad Godesberg in 1959, it rests on the unions, the workers, the big cities and a new generation of voters.

4.name: Deutsche Kommunistische Partei
4.text:
The German Communist Party was constituted in September 1968 as a legal successor in all but name to the KPD, which the Constitutional Court banned in 1956. Led by its chairman Kurt Bachmann and his deputy Herbert Mies, it ran in the 1969 federal election within the Action for Democratic Progress alliance and won a mere 0.6 percent.

The DKP follows the SED and the CPSU loyally, defends the invasion of Czechoslovakia, demands recognition of the GDR and the Oder-Neisse border and campaigns against NATO, the emergency laws and monopoly capital. It draws on veteran communists in the Ruhr, Hamburg and Bremen, works councils and a fresh intake of students. Its leverage lies in East Berlin's money, its discipline and its front organisations.

5.name: Sozialistischer Deutscher Studentenbund
5.text:
The Socialist German Student Union, cast out by the SPD in 1961, became the engine of the extra-parliamentary opposition that shook the Federal Republic in 1967 and 1968. Its charismatic leader Rudi Dutschke is still recovering in England from the assassination attempt of April 1968, its theorist Hans-Jürgen Krahl leads the Frankfurt remnant, and the federation is breaking up into rival cells and parties.

It preaches anti-authoritarian revolution against capitalism, the emergency laws, the Springer press and American imperialism in Vietnam, and it despises Soviet bureaucracy as much as Bonn. Some splinters are turning to violence: Andreas Baader and Gudrun Ensslin, convicted of the 1968 Frankfurt department-store arson, have gone underground. Its leverage lies in the universities and a radicalised youth.

6.name: Aktionsgemeinschaft Unabhängiger Deutscher
6.text:
The Action Community of Independent Germans was formed in 1965 around August Haußleiter, a veteran nationalist who left the CSU in 1949, and the remnants of his Deutsche Gemeinschaft. It gathers national neutralists, anti-nuclear campaigners and disillusioned conservatives who see the division of Germany as the joint work of both superpowers.

The AUD demands reunification through neutrality, the withdrawal of all foreign troops and the dissolution of both NATO and the Warsaw Pact, and it is ready to bargain with Moscow to achieve it. It denounces American cultural domination, the arms race and Bonn's dependence on Washington. Tiny at the polls, it draws on nationalists hostile to the Atlantic course and a scattering of rural and pacifist protesters.

7.name: Kommunistische Partei Deutschlands
7.text:
The Communist Party of Germany, banned by the Federal Constitutional Court in 1956, survives as an underground apparatus steered by the SED's West department in East Berlin under its first secretary Max Reimann. Its illegal cadres, couriers and secret printing shops kept the party alive through a decade of prosecutions and now form the hidden backbone of the new DKP.

The KPD regards the Federal Republic as a revanchist outpost of American imperialism and works for a socialist Germany on the model of the GDR under the leadership of the Soviet Union. It obeys East Berlin without question. Its leverage lies in conspiratorial discipline, SED and Stasi funding and the readiness of its veterans to serve as the core of a future people's democracy.

8.name: Anjoman-e Eslami-ye Daneshjuyan
8.text:
The Islamic Students' Associations unite devout Iranian students in West German university towns from Aachen and Bonn to Munich, part of a network of Muslim student societies spreading across Western Europe. They stand apart from the Marxist-dominated Confederation of Iranian Students and draw their inspiration from Mehdi Bazargan's banned Freedom Movement of Iran and the lectures of Ali Shariati in Tehran.

They seek an Iran freed from the Shah's dictatorship and from American tutelage, governed by a constitution and by an Islam reconciled with science, social justice and national independence, and they reject communism as firmly as clerical despotism. Their leverage lies in the future: engineers and doctors trained in Germany who will return home with these ideas.

9.name: Islamisches Zentrum Hamburg
9.text:
The Islamic Centre Hamburg, founded by Iranian merchants in the 1950s, opened its blue-tiled Imam Ali Mosque on the Alster in 1966 with the Shah's blessing. Under its director, the cleric Mohammad Beheshti, a product of the Qom seminaries and an admirer of the exiled Ayatollah Khomeini, it has become a meeting point for religious Iranian students across Europe; Beheshti is about to return to Iran.

Behind its respectable facade the circle around Beheshti works for an Iran ruled by Shia jurists, hostile to the Shah's secular monarchy, to American influence and to Israel, and scornful of communism. It organises students, preaches and keeps contact with the clergy of Najaf and Qom. Its leverage lies in its money, its prestige and the clerical network behind it.

10.name: Deutsche Muslim-Liga
10.text:
The German Muslim League was founded in Hamburg in the 1950s by German converts to Islam. It is one of the few organised voices of a Muslim minority that now numbers several hundred thousand, mostly Turkish guest workers, yet still lacks recognised religious bodies and has only a handful of real mosques, most of them built by foreign missions.

The League preaches an orthodox, law-abiding Islam, loyalty to the Basic Law, dialogue with the churches and close ties to the embassies of the Arab monarchies and the Saudi-backed Muslim World League. It shuns politics and revolution alike. Its leverage lies in its respectability, its contacts with officials and the patronage of wealthy Muslim states eager to sponsor mosques.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, is banned across the Arab world after repeated attempts to win over army officers for coups in Jordan. In West Germany, where thousands of Arab students attend the universities, its members find refuge from the Jordanian and Syrian secret police and spread their ideas in study circles.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and all existing Muslim governments and calls for a single caliphate that would unite the Muslim world under the sharia and stand against both American and Soviet power. It shuns open violence, relying on doctrine and patient infiltration. Its leverage in Germany is minimal, but its disciplined cadres carry its call back to the Middle East.

12.name: Islamische Gemeinschaft in Süddeutschland
12.text:
The Islamic Community of Southern Germany grew out of a commission formed in Munich in 1958 to build a mosque for Muslim émigrés, many of them Soviet Muslims who had served in the Wehrmacht's eastern legions. In the 1960s Said Ramadan, son-in-law of the Muslim Brotherhood's founder Hasan al-Banna, took it over with the backing of Arab students, and it is now raising money for an Islamic Centre in Munich-Freimann.

It embodies the Brotherhood's vision of a comprehensive Islam governing faith, society and politics, rejecting Arab socialism and atheist communism while condemning Western support for Israel. Its members are Arab students and professionals rather than workers. Its leverage lies in Gulf money, links to Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva and its ambition to speak for all German Muslims.

13.name: Deutsche Bundesbank
13.text:
The Deutsche Bundesbank, the central bank created in 1957, is by law independent of the federal government and guards the stability of the Deutsche Mark from its Frankfurt headquarters. On 1 January 1970 the banker Karl Klasen, a Social Democrat, succeeds Karl Blessing as its president, inheriting the aftermath of the bitter quarrel over the revaluation of the mark in October 1969.

Its council of central bankers sees itself as the true guardian of the economic miracle, above parties and above the temptations of electoral spending, trusting experts rather than majorities. It is neither Atlanticist nor neutralist, only obsessed with stability. Its leverage is decisive: by raising interest rates it can curb any government's reforms and discipline unions and employers alike.

14.name: Christlich-Soziale Union in Bayern
14.text:
The Christian Social Union is Bavaria's own party, allied with the CDU in a joint Bundestag group but fiercely independent, and it governs Bavaria alone under Minister-President Alfons Goppel. Its chairman Franz Josef Strauß, former Defence and Finance Minister and the most polarising politician in the land, now leads the charge against the new government from the opposition benches.

The CSU stands for Catholic values, Bavarian statehood, a strong defence and resistance to Ostpolitik, which it calls a sell-out of Germany's eastern territories. Strauß is a German Gaullist who distrusts American détente and dreams of a self-reliant Western Europe with its own nuclear weight. Its leverage lies in its Bavarian fortress, the farmers, the Catholic Church and the expellees.

15.name: Bundesverband der Deutschen Industrie
15.text:
The Federation of German Industries is the peak body of West German industry, speaking for the steel and coal barons of the Ruhr, the chemical giants, the carmakers and the family firms of the Mittelstand. Its president since 1949, the Sauerland industrialist Fritz Berg, was a confidant of Adenauer and works closely with the employers' confederation and the big banks.

The BDI defends the social market economy against the reforms of the new government, above all the unions' demand for parity co-determination on company boards, and it warns against wage drift after the wildcat strikes of September 1969. It funds the CDU and the FDP and lobbies discreetly. Its leverage lies in investment decisions, export power and its seat in Karl Schiller's Concerted Action.

16.name: Aktionsgemeinschaft Soziale Marktwirtschaft
16.english: Action Group for the Social Market Economy
16.text:
The Action Group for the Social Market Economy was founded in 1953 by ordoliberal economists around Alexander Rüstow to defend Ludwig Erhard's free-market order against cartels, planners and the expanding welfare state. With Erhard himself now a backbencher and Karl Schiller's Keynesian global steering in fashion, its economists, publicists and businessmen feel increasingly isolated.

It calls for competition, sound money, low taxes, private property and a lean state that sets the rules but stays out of the market, and it rejects both socialist planning and corporatist deals. Firmly Western, it sees economic freedom as the basis of political freedom. Its leverage lies in its intellectual standing, the Freiburg School tradition and its admirers in the FDP and the CDU business wing.

17.name: Deutscher Naturschutzring
17.text:
The German League for Nature Conservation, founded in 1950, is the umbrella of the country's conservation, hiking, hunting and homeland societies, with millions of members on paper. In 1970, European Conservation Year, its cause is gaining a new audience thanks to campaigners such as the zoologist Bernhard Grzimek, whose television programmes reach millions, and to the first national park in the Bavarian Forest, approved in 1969.

It calls for the protection of landscapes and species, clean rivers and air, curbs on pesticides and on the chemical industry, and limits to motorway and dam building. Politically neutral and largely conservative in temper, it has little cohesion. Its leverage lies in its broad membership and in the rising public alarm about pollution.

18.name: Jungsozialisten in der SPD
18.native_full: Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Jungsozialisten in der SPD
18.text:
The Young Socialists are the youth organisation of the SPD, embracing every party member under thirty-five. At their Munich congress in December 1969 they broke with their tame past, elected Karsten Voigt as chairman and declared themselves a socialist, anti-capitalist force within the governing party, absorbing many students of the 1968 revolt.

The Jusos back Brandt's Ostpolitik and reforms but demand far more: system-changing reforms, socialisation of key industries, democratic planning, co-determination everywhere and an end to the American war in Vietnam, in a Europe moving beyond the blocs. Their leverage lies in their numbers, their growing hold on local party branches and university towns, and their pressure on the Chancellor from within his own party.

19.name: Kommunistische Partei Deutschlands/Marxisten-Leninisten
19.text:
The Communist Party of Germany/Marxists-Leninists was founded in Hamburg on 31 December 1968 by Ernst Aust, a veteran KPD journalist who broke with Moscow over the Sino-Soviet split, and the circle around his paper Roter Morgen. It is the first of the new Maoist parties, drawing radicalised students and a few old communist workers.

It hails Mao Zedong and Enver Hoxha, denounces the Soviet Union as social-imperialist and the DKP as revisionist traitors, and calls for proletarian revolution and a socialist, reunified and independent Germany free of both superpowers. Riven by factional quarrels, it is small but fervent. Its leverage lies in the zeal of its cadres and the moral support of Beijing and Tirana.

20.name: Bund der Vertriebenen
20.text:
The Federation of Expellees speaks for the Germans driven from the eastern territories and Eastern Europe after 1945, claiming some two million members in regional associations from the Silesians to the Sudeten Germans. Its president Reinhold Rehs, who quit the SPD over its new Eastern policy, mobilises mass rallies against any recognition of the Oder-Neisse line.

The BdV denounces Brandt's Ostpolitik as betrayal, insists on the right to the homeland and the legal survival of the Reich within its 1937 borders, and rallies the national right within and beyond the Union parties. Fiercely anti-communist, it fuels resentment against a political class it accuses of renunciation. Its leverage lies in its votes, its press and its deputies.

21.name: Nationaldemokratische Partei Deutschlands
21.text:
The National Democratic Party of Germany was founded in 1964 as a rallying point for the scattered far right, uniting the old Deutsche Reichspartei, former Nazis and young nationalists. Under its chairman Adolf von Thadden it entered seven state parliaments, but in September 1969 it fell short of the Bundestag with 4.3 percent, a blow that has left it divided and demoralised.

The NPD preaches German nationalism, law and order, hostility to foreign workers, the restoration of the 1937 borders and an end to the guilt complex over the Nazi past, and it rejects both American and Soviet hegemony. Calls for a ban hang over it. Its leverage lies in militant youth, ex-soldiers, discontented farmers and a network of nationalist publishers.

22.name: Bundeswehr
22.text:
The Bundeswehr was founded in 1955 as the Federal Republic's contribution to NATO and has grown into a conscript army of nearly half a million men. Under Defence Minister Helmut Schmidt and Inspector General Ulrich de Maizière it faces a crisis of identity, as conscientious objectors multiply and a controversial study by the army inspector Albert Schnez calls for the reform of society itself.

Its officers, many of them Wehrmacht veterans, are bound by the doctrine of the citizen in uniform and civilian primacy, yet a conservative wing resents the permissive society, student protest and the new Ostpolitik. Fully integrated into NATO command, it regards the Soviet threat as existential. Its leverage lies in its size and its role as guarantor of national survival.

23.name: Haus Hohenzollern
23.text:
The House of Hohenzollern ruled Prussia and, from 1871 to 1918, the German Empire. Its head since 1951 is Prince Louis Ferdinand, grandson of Kaiser Wilhelm II, who once worked on Ford's assembly lines in Detroit and flew for Lufthansa. He lives at the Wümmehof near Bremen and guards the family seat of Hohenzollern Castle in Swabia, where the coffins of Frederick the Great and his father now rest.

Monarchism in the Federal Republic is a romantic fringe, but Louis Ferdinand, a cultured composer and friend of artists, embodies a Prussian tradition of service, duty and constitutional monarchy that some conservatives miss in the Bonn republic. Its leverage lies in prestige, Prussian nostalgia and the ties of the German aristocracy.
